extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) assessing prior art, public accessibility, anticipation, and related patentability issues under U.S. law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a reference qualifies as a 'printed publication' or prior art and for evaluating anticipation (35 U.S.C. 102) including public accessibility, dates of availability, admissions, use of multiple references, genus-species and range situations, and inherency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication public accessibility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is a 'printed publication' only if it is sufficiently accessible to the public to constitute prior art (public accessibility is the key inquiry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (In re Hall, In re Bayer, In re Klopfenstein) shows that ordinary library cataloging and shelving practices that render a document findable can make a thesis a printed publication; by contrast, shelving/indexing by student name without subject/title indexing (In re Cronyn) may not make a thesis publicly accessible. The examiner should assess whether the portion of the public concerned with the art would know of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing/searchability as a factor (but not necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing or searchability is not strictly necessary for a reference to be a printed publication, but it is one factor bearing on public accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voter Verified (quoting In re Lister) and Jazz Pharm. note that indexing is one among many factors and is no more or less important for online references than for tangible media. However, deficient indexing/searchability may weigh against public accessibility (see Acceleration Bay where website search/indexing was insufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Online database references — public accessibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A document in an online database is a printed publication only if it was publicly accessible such that an interested skilled artisan, using reasonable diligence, could have located it before the critical date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Acceleration Bay the court found that despite some indexing and search functionality, an artisan using reasonable diligence would not have been able to find the technical report because items were listed only by author or year, there were potentially hundreds of titles, and advanced search was unreliable. Thus technical accessibility alone is insufficient; practical ability to locate is required. See MPEP § 2128[I].

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral presentations with unrestricted written copies
rubrics_metrics.description: An orally presented paper can be a printed publication if written copies were disseminated without restriction to an audience open to all interested persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MIT v. AB Fortia: oral presentation to 50–500 persons with written copies distributed without restriction constituted a printed publication (six persons requested copies). Also note oral presentations and trade show demonstrations may be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as 'otherwise available to the public' (see MPEP § 2152.02(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internally distributed confidential documents are not printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents distributed only internally within an organization and intended to remain confidential are not printed publications, even if many copies were distributed, provided there is an existing confidentiality policy or agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere intent to remain confidential is insufficient unless there is a policy/understanding. Cases: In re George (in-house reports to those understanding confidentiality not printed publications); Northern Telecom (AESOP-B reports housed in restricted library not publicly accessible). Distribution to commercial companies without restriction can constitute publication (Garret Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public display can create printed publication status
rubrics_metrics.description: A publicly displayed document that persons of ordinary skill could see and were not precluded from copying can be a printed publication even if not disseminated by copies or indexed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Klopfenstein: factors for temporary displays include length of time displayed, expertise of target audience, reasonable expectations about copying, and ease of copying. Poster presentations/slides displayed at conferences for cumulative days were deemed publicly accessible. Medtronic and GoPro cases apply similar analyses and consider confidentiality expectations and nature of the meeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference/trade-show context factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing public accessibility at conferences or trade shows, consider the nature of the event, restrictions on disclosure, expectations of confidentiality, expectations about sharing, and the expertise of the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expertise of the target audience is relevant but not dispositive (GoPro). Trade shows are akin to conferences and directed to those interested in commercial/developmental aspects; materials presented at such venues can be prior art if reasonably available to interested persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of accessibility may be proved by routine business practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of routine business practices can be used to establish the date on which a publication became accessible to the public; specific evidence of the exact document’s availability is not always necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Constant v. AMD (undated specification sheets and company practice established accessibility timing); In re Hall (librarian affidavit on indexing/catalo­ging practices). But presuming inclusion in databases without evidence of general practices is speculative (In re Lister).

rubrics_metrics.name: Date a mailed publication is prior art — receipt rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A publication disseminated by mail is not prior art until it is received by at least one member of the public; the effective date is the receipt date, not mailing or publisher date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Schlittler: a magazine or journal is effective as prior art on the date when the first person receives it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions by applicant as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement by an applicant in the specification or during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission that can be relied upon for anticipation and obviousness determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Riverwood Int'l Corp. v. R.A. Jones; Constant v. AMD. However, if the admitted material is the applicant's own prior work, it may not be prior art absent a statutory basis; examiner must determine whether the subject matter is the applicant's own work or another's. Treat admissions as the work of another in absence of another credible explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion of prior art in the specification treated as admission
rubrics_metrics.description: When the specification identifies work done by another as 'prior art', that subject matter is treated as admitted prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Nomiya: labeling figures or material as 'prior art' is an admission that it is prior art relative to applicant's improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson-format claims imply admission of preamble as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting a claim in Jepson format is taken as an implied admission that the preamble subject matter is prior art of another, unless applicant provides a credible reason to the contrary or the preamble describes applicant's own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Fout held Jepson preamble to be admitted prior art; In re Ehrreich and Reading & Bates show the implication may be overcome with explanation (e.g., Jepson used to avoid double patenting) or if preamble describes applicant's own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: IDS listing is not an admission of prior art or materiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely listing a reference in an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) is not an admission that the reference is prior art or material to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Riverwood and 37 CFR 1.97(h) state that filing an IDS shall not be construed as an admission that the cited information is material to patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires every element in single reference
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated only if each and every element of the claim is found, either expressly or inherently, in a single prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil and Richardson v. Suzuki: elements must be arranged as required by the claim (not an ipsissimis verbis test — identical terminology not required). Multiple references may be permissible in some 102 contexts (see MPEP § 2131.01), but pure anticipation is single-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple references in 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections — permissible circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally one reference should be used for a 102 rejection, but multiple references may be cited to: (A) prove the primary reference contains an 'enabled disclosure', (B) explain the meaning of a term used in the primary reference, or (C) show that a characteristic not disclosed is inherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 2131.01 and cases (In re Samour, In re Donohue, Baxter Travenol) explain each circumstance: extra refs can show methods of making (enabled disclosure), extrinsic evidence can explain term meaning (but not expand it), or evidence can establish inherency (must show the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present and recognizable by persons of ordinary skill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving an 'enabled disclosure' via extra references
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra references and extrinsic evidence can be used to show the primary reference enables the claimed invention when the primary reference otherwise discloses the claimed composition/structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Samour and In re Donohue: publication taught claimed compound structure while patents taught methods of making such compounds; showing enablement of primary reference via secondary references is permissible and motivation to combine is not required for anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using extrinsic evidence to explain term meaning (but not expand it)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence may be used to explain the meaning of terms/phrases used in the primary reference but cannot be used to expand the reference’s meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Baxter Travenol Labs.: evidence (depositions, declarations, admissions) showed 'commercial blood bags' meant bags containing DEHP; such evidence explained but did not expand the primary reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using evidence to show inherency
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra references or evidence can be used to show a characteristic not expressly disclosed in the reference is inherent in the thing taught by the primary reference, but the evidence must show the missing matter is necessarily present and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continental Can v. Monsanto and Atlas Powder cases: inherency may be proven with test data and expert testimony; contemporaneous lack of recognition by skilled artisans does not preclude inherency findings. Extrinsic evidence need not predate the filing date if it shows a universal fact (see MPEP § 2124).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species anticipates genus
rubrics_metrics.description: A species disclosed in the prior art that falls within a claimed genus will anticipate the genus claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Slayter and In re Gosteli support that a specific species disclosed anticipates a broader genus claim (subject to priority issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming a claimed species anticipates regardless of listing size
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reference clearly names the claimed species, that species anticipates the claim no matter how many other species are named in the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte A and In re Sivaramakrishnan: even a comprehensive listing (e.g., Merck Index) that specifically names the compound or additive anticipates the species claim; being listed as representative or among many does not defeat anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic disclosure anticipates species if 'at once envisaged'
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic disclosure will anticipate a claimed species when the species can be 'at once envisaged' from the disclosure — i.e., a person of ordinary skill would immediately recognize the specific species from the generic teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanofi-Synthelabo, Osram Sylvania, Kennametal, In re Petering, In re Schauman: factors include size and limitation of the genus, preferred embodiments, ability to draw the structural formula or name the compound from the disclosure, and whether express contemplation of combinations exists. When arriving at a specific compound requires selecting and combining multiple lists of alternatives, anticipation requires that the classes be sufficiently limited or well delineated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation of ranges — specific example within claimed range
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific example in the prior art that falls within a claimed range anticipates the range claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titanium Metals v. Banner and In re Petering: an actual data point within the claimed range (e.g., graph point) is sufficient to anticipate a claimed compositional range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation of overlapping ranges requires 'sufficient specificity'
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art teaches a range overlapping or touching the claimed range but provides no specific examples within the claimed range, anticipation depends on whether the prior art discloses the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' (case-by-case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ClearValue v. Pearl River (narrow claimed range anticipated by broader prior range where no evidence of criticality across range) vs Atofina (broader prior range did not sufficiently describe a narrower claimed range where claimed range was shown to be critical). If insufficient specificity, the examiner should consider nonobviousness (evidence of unexpected results) and may issue a combined 102/103 rejection with reasoned statements on both anticipation and obviousness (Ex parte Lee). See MPEP § 2144.05 for obviousness of ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Values very close but non-overlapping do not anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art value or range that is very close to but does not overlap or touch the claimed range does not anticipate the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art does not disclose or sufficiently specify the claimed range, mere proximity of values without overlap is insufficient for anticipation; obviousness analysis may still be relevant.
